name: Memory Fundamentals
description: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, caches, allocation, garbage collection and the bugs that come from getting them wrong.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What Memory Fundamentals is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: RAM (memory) vs storage (disk)
cards.answer: RAM holds the data running programs are using right now — fast but volatile; storage (SSD or hard drive) keeps files permanently — larger and much slower.

right.title: Storage (SSD/HDD)
points: Typically hundreds of gigabytes to terabytes

cards.explanation: Opening a program copies it from storage into RAM. When RAM runs out, the OS can push some of it to disk ("swap"), which is why an overloaded machine suddenly becomes very slow.

cards.prompt: The stack vs the heap
cards.answer: The stack holds function call frames and local variables, managed automatically as functions are called and return; the heap holds data whose size or lifetime is not known in advance, allocated on request.

left.title: Stack
points: Automatic, freed when the function returns

right.title: Heap
points: Freed manually or by a garbage collector

cards.explanation: In Java, Python or JavaScript most objects live on the heap and the runtime cleans them up; in C you call `malloc` and `free` yourself; Rust and C++ free heap memory automatically when its owner goes out of scope.

cards.prompt: What is a memory address?
cards.answer: A number that identifies a location in memory, much like a house number on a street. Every variable and object lives at some address; a pointer or reference is a value that holds one.
cards.explanation: Addresses are usually shown in hexadecimal (`0x7ffd5e8c`). Python and Java hide raw addresses behind references; C and C++ let you work with them directly, which is powerful and error-prone.

cards.prompt: What is garbage collection?
cards.answer: Automatic memory management: the runtime finds objects the program can no longer reach and frees their memory, so programmers never call `free` themselves.
cards.explanation: Java, C#, Go, Python and JavaScript are garbage collected. It removes whole categories of bugs (use-after-free, double free) at the cost of extra CPU and memory and, in some designs, brief pauses.

cards.prompt: What is a memory leak?
cards.answer: Memory a program allocated and no longer needs but never releases, so its memory use keeps growing until it slows down or crashes.
cards.explanation: In C it is a missing `free`. Garbage-collected languages leak too, when something still references data you are done with — an ever-growing cache, a global list, an event listener never removed.

cards.prompt: What is the memory hierarchy?
cards.answer: The layers of storage from fastest and smallest to slowest and largest: CPU registers → L1/L2/L3 caches → RAM → SSD → hard disk/network. Each step down is roughly 10–1,000× slower and much larger.
cards.explanation: Programs run fast when the data they need is already in the upper layers. That is why accessing memory sequentially (which caches love) can be many times faster than jumping around randomly, even with the same Big-O.

modules.name: The Memory Model
modules.description: How a process sees memory, and what the hardware and OS are really doing underneath.

cards.prompt: Stack vs heap
cards.answer: The stack is a per-thread LIFO region managed automatically; the heap is a shared pool allocated and freed explicitly or by a GC.

left.title: Stack
points: Small and fixed (~1–8 MB per thread)

right.title: Heap
points: Allocator must find a suitable block
Large, limited by address space and RAM

cards.explanation: Stack overflow comes from deep recursion or huge locals; heap exhaustion from leaks or genuinely large data. Escape analysis in JIT compilers can promote a heap allocation to the stack when the object provably does not escape.

cards.prompt: What does virtual memory give you, and how does address translation work?
cards.answer: Each process gets its own address space, isolated from others. The MMU translates virtual pages to physical frames via page tables, cached in the TLB; a missing page triggers a page fault the OS resolves.
cards.explanation: Virtual memory buys isolation, relocation, demand paging, copy-on-write (how `fork` is cheap) and memory-mapped files. It costs a translation on every access — which is why TLB misses and huge pages matter for database and JVM performance.

cards.prompt: Roughly what do L1, L2, L3 and main memory cost in cycles, and why does that dominate performance?
cards.answer: L1 ~4 cycles, L2 ~12, L3 ~40, DRAM ~200–300 cycles. A single main-memory access can cost more than a hundred arithmetic operations, so cache misses — not instruction count — decide most real performance.
cards.explanation: Memory moves in cache lines (usually 64 bytes), so touching one byte pulls in 64. That is why iterating an array beats a linked list, why struct-of-arrays beats array-of-structs for column scans, and why false sharing between threads is so destructive.

resources.title: What every programmer should know about memory (Drepper)

cards.prompt: Two loops sum the same 2D array — one row-major, one column-major. Why can the column-major version be 5–10x slower?
cards.answer: Row-major traversal walks memory sequentially, using every byte of each cache line and letting the prefetcher work. Column-major jumps by the row stride, so each access touches a new line and most of every line is wasted.
cards.explanation: Spatial locality (nearby addresses soon) and temporal locality (same address soon) are the two levers. Loop interchange, blocking/tiling and choosing the right data layout routinely beat micro-optimising the arithmetic.

cards.prompt: On a typical 64-bit platform, what is `sizeof(S)`?
cards.answer: 12 bytes — 3 bytes of padding after `a` to align `b`, and 3 bytes of tail padding so arrays stay aligned. Reordering to `int, char, char` gives 8.
cards.explanation: Each member must sit at an address that is a multiple of its alignment, and the struct is padded to a multiple of its strictest member. Ordering fields largest-first is free memory savings in hot data structures.

modules.name: Allocation, GC & Bugs
modules.description: Allocators, collectors, leaks and the memory-safety failures behind most severe CVEs.

cards.prompt: Compare reference counting and tracing garbage collection.
cards.answer: Reference counting frees immediately when the count hits zero but cannot collect cycles and pays for every pointer update. Tracing GC periodically walks from roots and collects everything unreachable — handling cycles, at the cost of pauses and extra headroom.
cards.explanation: CPython uses reference counting plus a cycle detector; the JVM and .NET use tracing generational collectors; Swift uses ARC and asks you to break cycles with `weak`. Rust and C++ avoid both with ownership and RAII.

cards.prompt: You have a garbage collector. How can you still leak memory?
cards.answer: By keeping references alive: unbounded caches and collections, event listeners and callbacks never unregistered, static/global registries, thread-locals on pooled threads, and closures capturing large graphs.
cards.explanation: A GC frees the *unreachable*, not the *unused*. The fix is bounding lifetimes explicitly — size-limited caches, weak references where the key should drive the entry, and deregistration in teardown paths. Heap dumps plus dominator trees find them fast.

cards.prompt: What are use-after-free, double free and buffer overflow, and why do they matter for security?
cards.answer: Use-after-free reads or writes memory that has been returned to the allocator; double free corrupts allocator metadata; buffer overflow writes past an allocation's end. All are exploitable primitives that let an attacker corrupt adjacent state or hijack control flow.
cards.explanation: Microsoft and Google both report that roughly 70% of their severe CVEs are memory-safety bugs. Mitigations (ASLR, stack canaries, NX, CFI) raise the cost; memory-safe languages and sanitisers remove the class.

cards.prompt: What is memory fragmentation, and how do allocators fight it?
cards.answer: External fragmentation is free memory split into blocks too small to satisfy a request; internal is space wasted inside an allocated block. Allocators fight it with size classes, slab/arena allocation, coalescing of adjacent free blocks and compaction (where pointers can move).
cards.explanation: Long-running servers can exhaust memory with plenty free in total. Arena or pool allocators — allocate many objects, free the whole region at once — remove both fragmentation and per-object free cost, which is why they are common in games and compilers.

cards.prompt: When is `mmap` a better way to read a large file than `read`?
cards.answer: When you need random access to a large file and want the page cache to do the work: mapping avoids copying between kernel and user buffers and lets the OS page in only what you touch.
cards.explanation: The trade-offs: page faults are invisible latency, I/O errors surface as SIGBUS rather than a return code, and it is awkward for files that change size. Sequential streaming is usually just as fast with plain reads plus readahead.

modules.name: Allocators, Tools & the OS
modules.description: How malloc works, stack frames, copy-on-write, TLBs and huge pages, NUMA, OOM behaviour and leak-hunting tools.

cards.prompt: What does `malloc` actually do, and where does the memory come from?
cards.answer: A user-space allocator carves blocks out of larger regions it obtains from the kernel (`brk`/`sbrk` for the heap, `mmap` for large allocations). It keeps free lists or bins per size class, a small header per block, and per-thread caches to avoid lock contention.
cards.explanation: `free` usually returns memory to the allocator, not the OS, which is why RSS often stays high after a spike. Alternative allocators — jemalloc, tcmalloc, mimalloc — trade memory overhead for less fragmentation and better multithreaded throughput, and swapping one in is a common production fix.

resources.title: Wikipedia — C dynamic memory allocation — implementations

cards.prompt: What is in a stack frame, and why does deep recursion overflow?
cards.answer: Each call pushes a frame: the return address, saved registers, the previous frame pointer, spilled arguments and the function's local variables. The frame is popped on return. The stack is a fixed-size region per thread (commonly 1–8 MB), so enough nested frames exceed it.
cards.explanation: The frames are also what a debugger walks to print a stack trace and what a stack buffer overflow corrupts — overwriting the saved return address is the classic exploit, which stack canaries detect. Large local arrays belong on the heap for the same size reason.

cards.prompt: What is copy-on-write, and where does it show up?
cards.answer: Two users share the same memory pages marked read-only; only when one writes does the kernel (or runtime) copy the affected page for it. `fork` uses it so the child shares the parent's memory until either side modifies it.
cards.explanation: It also appears in filesystems and snapshots (ZFS, Btrfs, container image layers), Redis background saves, and immutable string or collection implementations. The catch: a forked process that then writes widely — or reference-count updates in CPython touching every object — triggers copying and memory growth.

cards.prompt: What is the TLB, and why do huge pages help large-memory workloads?
cards.answer: The translation lookaside buffer caches recent virtual-to-physical page translations. With 4 KB pages a large working set needs far more entries than the TLB holds, so misses force slow page-table walks. Huge pages (2 MB or 1 GB) cover the same memory with far fewer entries.
cards.explanation: Databases and JVMs with multi-gigabyte heaps benefit most. Transparent huge pages do it automatically but can cause latency spikes from compaction, which is why some databases recommend disabling THP and configuring explicit huge pages instead.

resources.title: Linux kernel docs — Transparent Hugepage Support

cards.prompt: What is NUMA, and why can a thread run slower on a bigger server?
cards.answer: Non-uniform memory access: on multi-socket machines each CPU socket has its own local memory, and reaching another socket's memory is noticeably slower. A thread scheduled on one socket but using memory allocated on another pays that penalty on every miss.
cards.explanation: NUMA-aware systems pin threads and allocate memory on the same node (`numactl`, first-touch allocation). Databases and high-performance services tune this; for most applications, keeping one process per socket or letting the kernel's automatic balancing work is enough.

cards.prompt: A container is killed with exit code 137 and no error in the application logs. What happened, and how do you confirm it?
cards.answer: It exceeded its cgroup memory limit and the kernel's OOM killer sent SIGKILL (128 + 9 = 137), which cannot be caught or logged by the process. Confirm with `kubectl describe pod` (reason OOMKilled), `dmesg`/`journalctl -k`, or container runtime events.
cards.explanation: Linux overcommits memory, so allocations succeed and the failure arrives later when pages are touched. Fixes: find the leak or peak usage, set runtime limits below the container limit (JVM `MaxRAMPercentage`, Node `--max-old-space-size`), and size requests and limits from measured usage.

resources.title: Kubernetes — Assign memory resources to containers

cards.prompt: Which tools find memory errors and leaks in native code, and which in managed runtimes?
cards.answer: Native: AddressSanitizer (out-of-bounds, use-after-free, with LeakSanitizer for leaks), Valgrind memcheck (slower, no recompile), and heap profilers such as heaptrack or jemalloc profiling. Managed: heap dumps analysed by dominator tree — Eclipse MAT for Java, dotnet-dump/dotMemory for .NET, Chrome DevTools heap snapshots for JavaScript, tracemalloc for Python.
cards.explanation: For a leak, compare two snapshots taken some time apart and look at what grew; the retaining path shows which reference keeps it alive. Run sanitizers in CI — they catch memory corruption when it happens instead of when it crashes much later.

cards.prompt: Manual memory management vs garbage collection vs ownership (Rust)
cards.answer: Manual (C, C++ raw) gives full control and no runtime cost but trusts the programmer; GC (Java, Go, C#, JS) removes use-after-free at the cost of pauses and memory headroom; ownership (Rust) proves safety at compile time with deterministic frees and no collector.

left.title: Manual / GC
points: Manual: fastest, and the source of most CVEs
GC: safe by default, easy to write
GC: pauses, headroom, finalisation is unpredictable

right.title: Ownership
points: Compiler tracks one owner per value
No GC, no use-after-free in safe code

cards.explanation: Each moves the cost somewhere: to bugs (manual), to runtime and memory (GC), or to learning and compile-time friction (ownership). Modern C++ with RAII and smart pointers sits between manual and ownership, but without compile-time guarantees.
